The second study (Li et al., 2020), which collected light levels from 235 urban intersections in Virginia, showed that an increase in the minimum horizontal illuminance of the intersection box is associated with a decrease in the night-to-day crash ratio by 2.9%. A meta-analysis study conducted based on 48 studies in 13 countries to evaluate the effects of providing lighting on previously unlit roads revealed a reduction of fatal accidents and injury by 60% and damage-only accidents by 15% due to roadway lighting (Elvik, 2009). An overview of field studies made by the Commission Internationale de l’Éclairage (CIE) showed a positive correlation between road lighting quality and road safety (CIE,1992). The average effect of the installation of road lighting based on 23 before-and-after studies was a 30% reduction in nighttime injury accidents. Wanvik (2009) analyzed injury accidents and property damage accidents on Dutch roads within a time window of two decades. The effect of roadway lighting on accident rates on all road types was estimated by odds ratio. The road lighting overall has an effect of reducing injury accidents during the hours of darkness by about 50%, and the effect during the hours of twilight is not as great as during the hours of darkness, but still reducing about one third of accidents. Not all studies that examined the effect of roadway lighting on nighttime crashes showed that lighting was associated with a reduction in the night crash frequency. One such study (van Schalkwyk et al., 2016) evaluating the presence of continuous mainline lighting on freeways did have a statistically significant reduction in night crash frequency on a highway in the state of Washington. This study, however, considered tangent sections of roadways and limited the analysis to lighting-related crashes only. To take roadway lighting into consideration, the national pedestrian crash report (Chang, 2008) divided dark hours into two categories, dark and dark but lighted. Beside these are daylight, dawn, and dusk. As showed in Figure 2, more than two-thirds of pedestrian fatalities occurred 6 when the light condition was either dark or dark but lighted, almost being evenly distributed between dark and dark but lighted. Of course, comparisons in terms of the number of fatalities carry less weight without knowing the number of road users and number of crashes. It should be expected that more pedestrians would be present in lighted areas during a dark period versus in unlighted areas and therefore more crashes in the dark but lighted category. As shown in Figure 3, further data analysis indicates that the worst light condition, dark, has the highest pedestrian fatality rate per police- reported pedestrian crash; and the best light condition, daylight, has the lowest pedestrian fatality rate per police-reported pedestrian crash.
